BMX5102 Business Analytics · Lesson 7 regression case

Fix the Queue First

A proposal for Legoland Malaysia's RM10 million · Peh Shao Hong (A0077294U)

To Mr. Sharif Ahmad, Managing Director From Business analyst, Legoland Malaysia Decision How to split RM10 million between renovation, facility upgrades and marketing Evidence Customer satisfaction survey, 500 families

About this page

Three tabs. Part 1 is the proposal to the Managing Director. Part 2 is the regression behind it, built step by step. Extra is Part 1 as a slide deck for senior management, with full screen and PDF export.

Purple notes. At the end of each Part 1 section, “The regression model at work” shows how the model is used to reach that section's numbers.

Charts. Generated in Python first, then converted to D3.js for interaction. Hover for values, press Table for the numbers; the Python original sits under each chart.

One limit. The survey has no cost or revenue data, so the ringgit split is a judgement built on the model.

Research objective

Find what makes a great day at Legoland Malaysia, and put the RM10 million behind it.

Situation
The borders have reopened, visitors are returning, and RM10 million is set aside to boost the business.
Where the park stands
Complication
The money can go to renovation, facility upgrades or marketing, and the survey shows they do not move satisfaction equally.
Why the choice matters
Question
Which parts of a visit lift overall satisfaction most, and for which visitors?
What the regression answers
Answer
Waiting time, for families with children. Fix the queues, protect what is already strong, then market.
What this page proposes

The recommendation

Put RM6 million into waiting time, RM2.5 million into keeping rides and cleanliness strong, and RM1.5 million into marketing to families, in that order.

  • Why. Waiting time is the park's lowest score, 70 out of 100, and each point of it is worth +0.73 overall to families with children against +0.23 to other visitors
  • What it takes. To bring the average family from 55.8 to 65 overall, the model needs about +7.4 points on waiting time with +3 on rides and +2 on cleanliness. Park-wide that is worth +8.0 (95% interval 7.4 to 8.5)
  • How it is protected. The queue budget is released in two stages with the survey re-run in between, a cost rule says when to move money between the levers, and marketing waits until the queues can take more visitors

What the survey cannot tell us: what a point of improvement costs, or what it earns. It has no cost, revenue or repeat-visit fields, so the split is indicative and the first stage is a test.

The proposal comes first. Sections 2 to 5 then show how its numbers were reached: three findings from the survey, and the model put to work. The model behind all of it explains 80% of the variation in overall satisfaction; how it was built and checked is in Part 2.

1

The proposal: RM10 million in three moves

Three ways to spend it, the one recommended, what the model expects in return and how to tell. Sections 2 to 5 then show where each number comes from.

Option 1

Spread it evenly

Split the budget across renovation, facilities and marketing, with something for every part of the park.

Against it: it funds games (+0.10 per point) on the same footing as queues (+0.73 per point for families). An 8-point lift in games is worth +0.8; a 10-point lift in waiting time is worth +5.8.

Recommended Option 2

Fix the queue first

Put 60% into waiting time, hold cleanliness and ride quality where they are strong, and market to families once the queues can take them.

For it: it leans on the only lever with the room to reach 65 for families, and it is worth the most to the core customer. Against it: the survey cannot price a point of waiting-time satisfaction, so the first stage has to be a test.

Option 3

Build a headline ride

Spend most of the budget on one major new attraction and advertise it.

Against it, for now: a headline ride at this park was estimated at more than RM40 million in 2016, four times this budget. Rides alone would also have to average more than 100 out of 100 to reach the goal, and a popular new ride risks longer queues. It is the right second move, after the queues are under control.

Why each share is the size it is

The survey has no cost data, so the amounts cannot be calculated from it. Each share follows the size of the job the model gives that lever, and each implies a price that supplier quotes can confirm or overturn.

LeverShareWhy this sizeThe price it impliesWhat would change it
Waiting timeRM6.0m (60%)It has to supply 5.4 of the 9.2 points families need (59%) and 54% of the park-wide gain, and it is the only lever that needs both new systems and building workAbout RM0.8 million per waiting-time pointIf quotes price the 7.4 points for less, the saving moves to cleanliness and rides, which are worth more per point across all visitors
RidesRM1.5m (15%)A refresh of existing rides for 3 points on a score already at 86, not a new rideRM0.5 million per rides pointA quote well above this turns the refresh into maintenance only
CleanlinessRM1.0m (10%)Worth the most per point but with the least room, so it is the smallest job: 2 pointsRM0.5 million per cleanliness pointIf more points are on offer near this price, buy them first: each one replaces 1.28 waiting-time points for families
Families campaignRM1.5m (15%)The smallest modelled pay-off, +1.6 on the park average per ten points of visitor mix, and it has to wait for the queues–Run it as a test and scale it only if bookings respond

Two public reference points for scale. A headline attraction at this park, LEGO NINJAGO The Ride, was estimated at more than RM40 million in 2016, so the whole RM10 million is about a quarter of a new ride. Its LEGO Star Wars Miniland display cost more than RM6 million in 2014, so the queue budget is the size of one mid-sized attraction. Virtual queuing is established technology, in use at Legoland Windsor among some 40 parks by 2013. These are historical figures for scale, not quotes.

What could go wrong, and the safeguard

RiskWhy it mattersSafeguard built into the proposal
The link may not be cause and effectHappier families may simply rate everything higher, queues includedRelease the queue budget in two stages and re-run the survey in between. Each point gained on waiting time should bring about 0.73 on overall for families (the model's 95% range is 0.66 to 0.81); if it does not, stop
The prices behind the split may be wrongThe split assumes about RM0.8 million per waiting-time point and RM0.5 million per rides or cleanliness point, and the survey has no cost dataGet quotes before stage 2. Across all visitors, cleanliness and rides are worth more per point, so any further points on offer near the assumed price are bought first. If a waiting-time point is quoted below about 62% of a cleanliness point, waiting time is the better buy outright
Marketing could make queues worseMore visitors on the same rides means longer waits, the thing families punish mostSequence it: queues first, campaign after
Only visitors were surveyedNothing here measures why other families stay awayTreat the marketing share as a test budget and track bookings separately

Why waiting time and not cleanliness. Per point, cleanliness is worth more. But to reach the goal on its own it would have to average 98 out of 100, a score only 4% of families give today. Waiting time has to reach 82, which 13% already give. Raising rides and cleanliness together instead would take about 5.9 points on each, from scores already in the high 80s. The plan therefore asks most of waiting time and a little of the other two.

Why in that order. Marketing that works brings more visitors, and more visitors on the same rides means longer waits. Spending on the campaign before the queues are fixed would buy growth at the expense of the customers the park most needs to keep happy.

How the two stages work. Stage 1 commits half of the queue budget, RM3.0 million, to the busiest rides. Six months on, the same survey is run again. If families' waiting-time score has risen and their overall score has followed at about 0.73 points per point, stage 2 is released. If not, the remaining money is held.

What stays a judgement. The model supplies the goal, the targets and the expected gains. It cannot supply the ringgit amounts: those rest on the implied prices above being confirmed by quotes, with the cost rule in section 5 deciding any change. The +3 on rides and +2 on cleanliness are assumed, modest gains on scores that are already high.

The regression model at work

Every target and expected gain in this section is the equation below applied to a stated move. Highlighted terms are the ones used. The model is built in Part 2, section E and checked in section F.

overall = −119.44 + 0.617·rides + 0.096·games + 0.940·clean + 0.027·distance + 0.226·wait + HasChild × (−19.71 + 0.508·wait)
  • The waiting-time target. The equation solved backwards for the goal of 65: (65 − 55.85 − 3 × 0.617 − 2 × 0.940) ÷ 0.734 = 7.4 points. Section 5 shows it step by step.
  • Expected change = coefficient × move. Waiting time for families: 7.4 × (0.226 + 0.508) = +5.4. Rides: 3 × 0.617. Cleanliness: 2 × 0.940. Each is averaged over the 500 families with ratings capped at 100, which gives +1.8 and +1.8 for the last two.
  • The 95% intervals. Each gain is a weighted sum of coefficients, so its interval comes from the coefficients' standard errors (statsmodels t_test).
  • The test for stage 2. The family waiting-time slope, 0.734 with a 95% interval of 0.66 to 0.81, is the prediction the repeat survey is judged against.
  • The cost rule. A ratio of two coefficients: cleanliness 0.940 ÷ waiting time across all visitors 0.581 = 1.62.
2

Families with children are the park's happiest visitors, however many children they bring

Where the numbers come from, finding 1. It says whom the money should serve.

Families with children are 70% of the visitors surveyed and the customers the park is built for. They score it 55.8 overall against 40.7 for visitors without children. At the same ratings for rides, games, cleanliness and an average wait, the model still puts a family 15.8 points higher.

One child or five makes no difference, so the budget does not need to treat small and large families differently. The park already works for its target customer. The budget should make it work better for them, and marketing should bring in more of them.

The regression model at work

This section rests on the HasChild switch: a 0/1 dummy that moves the starting point and, through the interaction, the waiting-time slope. The model is built in Part 2, section E and checked in section F.

overall = −119.44 + 0.617·rides + 0.096·games + 0.940·clean + 0.027·distance + 0.226·wait + HasChild × (−19.71 + 0.508·wait)
  • Children as a yes/no. The model ladder tried children as a count, as six categories and as one yes/no (Part 2, section D). One dummy fits as well as five (F-test p = 0.81), so HasChild is a single switch.
  • The family premium. With HasChild = 1 the equation adds −19.71 + 0.508 × wait. At the average waiting-time score of 69.9: −19.71 + 0.508 × 69.9 = +15.8 points, with rides, games, cleanliness and distance held equal.
  • What the chart is. Plain averages from the survey (40.7 and 55.8). The model's job here is to confirm the step survives once the other drivers are held equal, which it does.
3

Waiting time is the weakest score in the park, and it is worth three times as much to families

Where the numbers come from, finding 2. It says which lever to pull.

70
Average waiting-time score, the lowest of the four ratings (rides 86, cleanliness 88, games 79)
+0.73
Overall points per waiting-time point, families with children (95% interval 0.66 to 0.81)
+0.23
Overall points per waiting-time point, visitors without children
+7.3
Overall points for a family if its waiting-time score rises by 10

Queues are where the park loses its best customers. At the lowest waiting-time scores a family is barely happier than a visitor with no children at all. A family that rates it well is the happiest visitor in the data. Good queues are what turn the core customer into a delighted one.

Waiting-time scores are the same on weekends and weekdays (69.9 against 69.9), and a point is worth the same on either, so this is not a peak-day problem that scheduling alone can solve. It is also the rating with the widest spread between families, which means some visits already go well and the others can be brought up to them.

The regression model at work

This section reads the two waiting-time terms: the base slope and the interaction that changes it for families. The model is built in Part 2, section E and checked in section F.

overall = −119.44 + 0.617·rides + 0.096·games + 0.940·clean + 0.027·distance + 0.226·wait + HasChild × (−19.71 + 0.508·wait)
  • +0.23 for visitors without children. The coefficient on wait, 0.226. It is the base group's slope (HasChild = 0).
  • +0.73 for families. Base slope plus the interaction: 0.226 + 0.508 = 0.734, 95% interval 0.66 to 0.81.
  • A 10-point rise. 10 × 0.734 = +7.3 overall for a family; 10 × 0.226 = +2.3 for other visitors.
  • The two lines in the chart. The equation drawn with rides, games, cleanliness and distance fixed at their averages, once with HasChild = 0 and once with HasChild = 1.
  • The gap between the lines. −19.71 + 0.508 × 55 = +8.2; −19.71 + 0.508 × 85 = +23.5.
  • Same on weekends. A wait × weekend term was added to the model and rejected (F-test p = 0.57).
4

Cleanliness and rides matter but are already strong; games, weekends and distance barely move the result

Where the numbers come from, finding 3. It says what to protect and what to leave alone.

LeverAverage score nowTypical spread (SD)Overall points per rating pointOverall points per SD
Waiting time, families with children69.710.8+0.73+7.9
Cleanliness87.95.1+0.94+4.8
Rides85.85.5+0.62+3.4
Waiting time, no children70.310.8+0.23+2.4
Games78.78.1+0.10+0.8

Protect cleanliness. It has the largest effect per point, +0.94, and already scores 88. There is little room to gain and a lot to lose: letting it slip five points would cost about 4.7 overall for every visitor.

Keep the rides reliable. Rides are worth +0.62 per point and score 86. A modest refresh earns its place; a headline new ride does not, yet.

Leave games alone. At +0.10 per point, even a 5-point improvement in games would add only 0.5 overall.

Weekends and distance are not levers. Weekend visitors are no more or less satisfied. Families who travel further are, if anything, very slightly happier, so distance is no barrier to marketing across the border.

The regression model at work

This section compares the remaining coefficients, first per rating point and then per standard deviation so that levers with different spreads can be set side by side. The model is built in Part 2, section E and checked in section F.

overall = −119.44 + 0.617·rides + 0.096·games + 0.940·clean + 0.027·distance + 0.226·wait + HasChild × (−19.71 + 0.508·wait)
  • Per rating point. Read straight off the equation: cleanliness 0.940, rides 0.617, games 0.096.
  • Per standard deviation. Coefficient × the rating's standard deviation. Waiting time for families 0.734 × 10.8 = 7.9; cleanliness 0.940 × 5.1 = 4.8; rides 0.617 × 5.5 = 3.4; games 0.096 × 8.1 = 0.8.
  • Letting cleanliness slip. 5 points × 0.940 = 4.7 overall, for every visitor.
  • Weekend. It was in the model and dropped: coefficient −0.16, p = 0.80, so it is not in the equation.
  • Distance. Coefficient +0.027 per unit: small and positive, so travelling further does not lower satisfaction. It leans on a few long trips (Part 2, section F).
5

Run backwards, the model says waiting time is the only lever with the room to carry the average family to 65

The model put to work. The equation is run backwards (what would it take?) and forwards (what if?) for all 500 families. This is where the goal, the targets and the expected gains in section 1 come from.

65.1
Overall score of the 177 families who rate the wait at or above today's average of 70
46.4
Overall score of the 172 families who rate the wait below 70
65
The goal for the average family: the level the first group already reports. Today it is 55.8
+9.2
Overall points the average family still has to gain

Why 65?

It is what the park already delivers. The 177 families who rate the wait at or above the average score the park 65.1 overall, and 30% of all families already score it 65 or higher. Those 177 families differ from the average family by +8.7 on waiting time, +1.5 on rides and +1.6 on cleanliness, and the model accounts for 9.0 of the 9.2-point gap between them. So the goal is to bring the average family to where the better-served half already are, and the plan asks for a comparable shift, a little less on waiting time and a little more on the other two: +7.4, +3 and +2.

Backwards: how far would each lever have to move?

A coefficient is a rate, so it can be turned round. Lift needed = points to find ÷ overall points per rating point. For waiting time that is 9.2 ÷ 0.734 = 12.5 points.

Forwards: what if?

What one point of each lever is worth

LeverOverall per point, familiesOverall per point, all visitorsWorth in waiting-time pointsAverage score nowRoom left to 100
Waiting time+0.73+0.581.0069.930.1

Rides+0.62+0.621.0685.814.2

A rule that stands in for the missing cost data. Across all visitors, one cleanliness point is worth 1.62 waiting-time points. So per ringgit, waiting time wins only when a waiting-time point costs less than about 62% of a cleanliness point; otherwise cleanliness is the better buy for as long as it has room to rise. It has 12 points of room against 30 for waiting time, which is why the plan buys a little cleanliness first and asks waiting time for the rest. Supplier quotes turn this into a decision.

A test for any new ride. For families, a ride point is worth 0.84 waiting-time points. A new attraction that lifts ride satisfaction by 5 pays off only if it costs families less than 4.2 points of waiting-time satisfaction.

Marketing, put through the model. At today's ratings a family scores 15.8 points above a visitor without children. Moving ten points of the visitor mix towards families would lift the park average by about 1.6 with no change to the park itself. That is real but smaller than the queue work, which is why marketing is the smallest of the three budget categories.

What the model can and cannot promise. For the average family, the waiting-time part of the plan moves the model's expectation from 55.8 to 61.3, each known to within about a point. For any one family the 95% range is about ±14. The model is a tool for averages over many visits, not for promising one visitor's score. It is also a straight line: a waiting-time point is worth the same from 50 as from 85, so aiming at the worst queues is justified by where the unhappy families are, not by a bigger pay-off per point.

The regression model at work

This section uses the whole equation as a tool: solved backwards for a goal, run forwards for scenarios, and its coefficients compared with one another. The model is built in Part 2, section E and checked in section F.

overall = −119.44 + 0.617·rides + 0.096·games + 0.940·clean + 0.027·distance + 0.226·wait + HasChild × (−19.71 + 0.508·wait)
  • Backwards. Lift needed = points to find ÷ coefficient. The average family has 65 − 55.85 = 9.15 points to find. Waiting time 9.15 ÷ 0.734 = 12.5; cleanliness 9.15 ÷ 0.940 = 9.7; rides 9.15 ÷ 0.617 = 14.8.
  • The recommended route. (9.15 − 3 × 0.617 − 2 × 0.940) ÷ 0.734 = 7.4 waiting-time points.
  • Forwards. Each scenario changes the ratings of the 500 surveyed families, re-predicts their overall score with the equation, and averages the change.
  • The intervals. The average change is a weighted sum of coefficients, so statsmodels t_test gives its 95% interval from their standard errors.
  • The exchange rate. Waiting-time slope across all visitors = 0.226 + 0.698 × 0.508 = 0.581. Cleanliness in waiting-time points = 0.940 ÷ 0.581 = 1.62.
  • Marketing mix. 0.10 × the family premium at the average wait (15.8) = 1.6 on the park average.
  • One family versus the average. The confidence interval for the mean and the wider prediction interval for one family both come from get_prediction on the fitted model.

The regression behind Part 1, built step by step: define the variables, explore, check for overlapping drivers, climb the model ladder, read the final model, run the four diagnostic charts, look for influential points, record what was changed, and state the limits.

A

What is in the survey?

Step 1: name the one outcome, list the drivers, and say which drivers are categories.

500 families answered the marketing department's survey. One row is one family's visit. There are no missing values. The outcome is the overall satisfaction score; the other seven fields are candidate drivers of it.

The eight fields

FieldRoleTypeRange in the dataAverageWhat it is
overallOutcome (Y)number, 0–1006 to 10051.3Overall satisfaction score
ridesDriver (X)number, 0–10072 to 10085.8Satisfaction with the rides
gamesDriver (X)number, 0–10057 to 10078.7Satisfaction with the games
waitDriver (X)number, 0–10040 to 10069.9Satisfaction with the waiting time for activities
cleanDriver (X)number, 0–10074 to 10087.9Satisfaction with the cleanliness of the park
distanceDriver (X)number, unit not stated0.5 to 239.231.0 (median 19.0)Distance the family travelled to the park
num.childDriver (X)count, modelled as a category0 to 5151 families with noneNumber of children the family brought
weekendDriver (X)category: yes / no241 yes, 259 nobase level: noWhether the visit was on a weekend

Checks before any model

  • The real file is in use: 500 rows and 8 columns, not a dummy copy
  • Direction is right: the ratings, the trip and the family describe the visit, and overall is the verdict on it. Causes on X, outcome on Y
  • Every rating stays inside 0 to 100. Only 1 family scored 100 overall and 3 scored 10 or below, so the scale's limits are not distorting the fit
  • weekend is a text category and enters as C(weekend), base level “no”

Three things to keep in mind

  • These are ratings, not measurements. “wait” is how satisfied the family felt about queueing, not minutes spent in a queue.
  • Distance has no unit. The data dictionary does not say kilometres or miles, so this page says “units”.
  • Only visitors were asked. The survey cannot speak for families who chose not to come.
B

What do the answers look like?

Step 2: plot every distribution and the outcome against every driver before fitting anything.

Key findings

Three things to carry into the model.

  • Distance is lognormal, so its log is worth trying. Section D reports the fit both ways
  • Children act like a yes/no category. A count would force a staircase onto a single step
  • No curves in the ratings. Straight lines look like the right shape for all four

Rides and cleanliness move together, r = 0.79: families who like the rides also rate the park clean. Their VIFs are 2.69 and 2.98, under the course threshold of 5, so both stay in the model and their coefficients can be read.

Key findings

Unlike the class example, the interaction model wins here.

  • The children step lifts adjusted R² from 0.679 to 0.774. One yes/no does the work of five dummies
  • The waiting-time interaction lifts it again to 0.799, and the F-test is decisive (p < 0.001). The chart in Part 1, section 3 is this model drawn
  • Nothing else earns a place. No curve, no weekend effect, no second interaction survives its test

A judgement call: merging rides and cleanliness is statistically defensible (p = 0.086). They are kept apart because the budget has to choose between them.

E

The final model

Step 5: the equation with its numbers, then every driver read as a rate with units.

Every sign makes business sense. Better rides, cleaner grounds, shorter-feeling queues and better games all go with higher overall satisfaction. Nothing has a sign that contradicts common sense, which is one more indication that the overlap between rides and cleanliness is not distorting the coefficients.

The negative has-child coefficient is not bad news. When a group has its own slope, its dummy is the gap at a waiting-time score of zero, a place no family occupies. At the average waiting-time score of 70, a family with children is 15.8 points happier overall than a visitor without, at the same ratings.

What a p-value below 0.05 means here. If a driver truly had no relationship with overall satisfaction, the chance of seeing a coefficient this strong in a sample of 500 would be below 5%. For rides, cleanliness and both waiting-time terms it is below 0.1%.

A cross-check. Fitting the two groups separately gives waiting-time slopes of 0.22 and 0.74, against 0.23 and 0.73 in the final model. The small differences arise because the final model lets only the waiting-time slope differ between the two groups. The equation above is two honest straight lines, not an artefact of the formula.

The five most influential families

Course convention: Cook's D above 0.1 is a potential outlier, above 0.5 is extreme. The largest here is 0.021, so no single family steers the line. Three of the five rated every part of the park below average and then scored it 6 or 7 overall, where the model expected about 22. Nothing in the file suggests a data-entry error; they read as visitors for whom something outside the four ratings went wrong, which is a reason to keep them, not remove them.

The coefficients barely move and the ranking of the levers is unchanged, so no family is removed. One weaker spot is worth stating: the distance effect leans on 10 families who travelled more than 150 units. Without them its coefficient falls to 0.015 and is no longer significant (p = 0.24). Distance stays in the model, but no recommendation rests on it.

H

What this analysis cannot tell us

Step 8: limitations first, then a red-flag checklist with the result of each check.

Limitations

  • One fifth is unexplained. R² is 0.80, and the typical miss is about 7 points. Food, prices, weather, crowding and staff are not in the survey.
  • Correlation is not causation. All the ratings come from the same questionnaire, so a family in a good mood may score everything higher. The coefficients show what moves together with overall satisfaction, not what is guaranteed to follow a change.
  • The lines only hold inside the data. Waiting-time scores run from 40 to 100, rides from 72, cleanliness from 74. The model should not be used to predict below those, and every scenario in Part 1 stays inside them.
  • No cost, revenue or repeat-visit data. The model ranks the levers by satisfaction. It cannot say which gives the best return per ringgit, or what a satisfaction point is worth in ticket sales.
  • Visitors only. The survey says nothing about families who stayed away, so it cannot measure what marketing would bring in.
  • Two weak drivers. Games is only just significant (p = 0.040), and the distance effect depends on 10 long trips.

Red-flag checklist

  • Real file used. 500 rows; R² is 0.80, not a suspicious 1.0
  • Y is the outcome. Overall satisfaction on the left, the parts of the visit on the right
  • Distributions plotted. Distance is lognormal; its log was tried and did not improve the fit, so raw distance is kept (section G)
  • Correlation matrix and VIF checked. Largest VIF 2.98; rides and clean flagged at r = 0.79
  • Every sign makes business sense. All drivers positive; the has-child dummy explained as the gap at wait = 0
  • Insignificant drivers dropped. Weekend (p = 0.80); three extra interactions (p = 0.61)
  • Adjusted R² used for every model comparison, alongside nested F-tests
  • All four diagnostic charts interpreted and each pattern named
  • Cook's distance checked. Largest 0.021; with and without the top five reported
  • Base levels named. has-child base = no, weekend base = no; dummy and interaction read as intercept shift and slope shift
  • Log rule. No logged term is in the final model, so every coefficient reads as points per unit
  • Translated into a decision. Part 1, section 1 for the decision, and section 5 for the model run backwards for the target and forwards for the expected gain
+

Part 1 as a slide deck for senior management

11 slides, one point each. The charts are the same live D3 charts as in Part 1, so hovering still works while presenting.

Arrow keys or a click to move · F for full screen · the PDF button opens Print: choose “Save as PDF” for one slide per page

The deck follows Part 1 in the same order: the recommendation, the three findings, the goal and what it takes, the return, the money, the risks, and the test. One backup slide carries the model. For presenting or exporting, open it in its own tab.

Data. Legoland.csv, the customer satisfaction survey supplied with the case: 500 families, 8 fields, no missing values. num.child is renamed num_child in code; has_child is derived from it (yes when the family brought at least one child).

Method. Ordinary least squares with the statsmodels formula API. Final model: overall ~ rides + games + clean + distance + wait * C(has_child). Nested models compared with anova_lm; diagnostics from lmdiag; influence from Cook's distance; scenario intervals from t_test on the fitted coefficients. Charts are drawn in Python with matplotlib, seaborn and lmdiag, then redrawn in D3.js from the same computed values so they can be hovered.

External references. Legoland Malaysia press release, 27 June 2016 (LEGO NINJAGO The Ride, more than RM40 million). New Straits Times (LEGO Star Wars Miniland, more than RM6 million, opened September 2014). TTG Asia, 12 June 2013 (virtual queuing at Legoland Windsor and other parks). Used for scale only.

Reading the budget tables. The goal, the targets and the expected changes come from the final model: coefficients multiplied by the stated moves, with 95% intervals from the uncertainty in the coefficients. They assume the relationships are causal. The ringgit shares and the two-stage release are the analyst's judgement, to be tested against supplier quotes and the repeat survey.
